program.title: Work and its sign
program.learning_goal: Decide whether a force adds energy, removes energy, or does no work.

core1a.title: A guide: the moving crate
core1a.authored_question: A 10 N friction force acts left while a crate slides 3 m right. What work does friction do?
walkthrough_steps: Choose the motion direction: 3 m right.
Choose the force direction: 10 N left.
Calculate W = 10 × 3 × cos 180° = −30 J.
Interpret the sign: friction removes mechanical energy from the moving crate.
core1a.conditions: Constant 10 N force, straight 3 m displacement, and no change of force direction within this step.

core1b.title: Your turn: two journeys
core1b.authored_question: A robot travels 4 m to the right while a 6 N braking force acts left. It then travels 2 m to the left while a 4 N resistive force acts right. What is the combined work done by these two resistive forces?
core1b.change_of_conditions: Two sequential displacement directions; requires tracking the sign twice rather than copying one-step friction arithmetic.

program.scope_note: For change of kinetic energy per distance, the relevant force is net tangential force; source Q7 wording remains unqualified.

program.title: Momentum and kinetic energy
program.learning_goal: Explain why equal momentum does not imply equal kinetic energy.

core1a.title: A guide: a toy trolley’s energy
core1a.authored_question: A 2 kg toy trolley has momentum 6 kg·m/s. How much kinetic energy does it have?
walkthrough_steps: Find the speed v=p/m=6/2=3 m/s.
Find kinetic energy K=½mv²=½×2×3²=9 J.
Check using K=p²/(2m)=36/4=9 J.
Compare the same 2 kg trolley at momentum magnitudes 0, 2, 6 and 10 kg·m/s: kinetic energies 0, 1, 9 and 25 J; a curved, not linear, K-versus-p relationship.
core1a.conditions: Classical, nonrelativistic momentum; the stated momentum and mass are measured in one inertial frame.

core1b.title: Your turn: two mystery toy carts
core1b.authored_question: A class measures two toy carts. Cart A has mass 2 kg and momentum magnitude 4 kg·m/s. Cart B has mass 4 kg and momentum magnitude 8 kg·m/s. Which cart has more kinetic energy, and by how much?
core1b.change_of_conditions: Unlike the guide's single trolley or fixed-mass table, both momentum and mass change. The learner must select K=p²/(2m) for each and compare resulting values, rather than apply one fixed-variable rule.

program.scope_note: Q2, Q4 and Q8 theme grouping, learner-facing candidate only; guided same-mass pattern table, same-energy and same-momentum boundaries; no QRT classification assigned.

program.title: Energy and motion
program.learning_goal: Find kinetic energy and possible heights on a smooth path, understand K=0 turning points, and distinguish changes with time from changes with height.

core1a.title: A guide: a toy cart climbing a ramp
core1a.authored_question: A 2 kg toy cart has 80 J of total mechanical energy on a smooth ramp. When it reaches a height of 2 m, how fast is it going? Take g = 10 m/s².
walkthrough_steps: Use U=mgh=2×10×2=40 J at height 2 m.
Compute K=E−U=80−40=40 J; then v=√(2K/m)=√40≈6.3 m/s.
Compare other locations on the same ramp: h=0 gives K=80 J, h=4 gives K=0, and h=5 is impossible because U would exceed E.

Model a separate ball launched straight upward at 20 m/s with constant g=10 m/s² and no drag: at t=1 s its vertical velocity is 10 m/s and rise is 15 m; at t=2 s its velocity is zero and rise is 20 m. Velocity changes equally each second, not for every metre.
core1a.conditions: Smooth ramp with no friction, no mechanical energy loss, zero height reference, g=10 m/s² constant; vertical-ball example assumes no drag.

core1b.title: Your turn: can the cart reach the flag?
core1b.authored_question: A 1 kg toy cart starts in a valley at height 1 m with 50 J of total mechanical energy. The finish flag is at a height of 3 m, but to get there the cart must first cross a hilltop 6 m high. The track is smooth, with no motor or friction. Take g = 10 m/s². Can the cart reach the flag?
core1b.change_of_conditions: Guide: single ramp with a height–energy table and a separate vertical-flight comparison. Challenge: determine accessibility of a finish beyond an intervening hilltop; the learner must check whole-path energy rather than only final height.

program.scope_note: Original Q5/Q6/Q9 remain unverified source themes, not repeated learner-facing tasks. Simplified child-facing teaching candidate; Q9 must allow K=0.

program.title: Potential energy and force
program.source_gate_note: Source wording omits the minus sign
program.learning_goal: Find direction and magnitude of a one-dimensional conservative force from how potential energy changes with position, including a flat interval and sharp-corner limitation.

core1a.title: A guide: follow a sloping energy line
core1a.authored_question: On a straight track, a particle’s potential energy is 12 J at x = 0 m and 6 J at x = 2 m. The graph is a straight line. What force acts along the track?
walkthrough_steps: Read U(0 m)=12 J and U(2 m)=6 J; find the slope ΔU/Δx=(6−12)/(2−0)=−3 J/m=−3 N.
Use Fₓ=−dU/dx for a one-dimensional conservative force; a straight segment has Fₓ=−(slope)=+3 N, directed right.
Contrast three line shapes: rising slope means force left, flat slope means zero force, falling slope means force right.
Explain that a sharp corner does not have a unique ordinary derivative at the join; the force can still be calculated separately on open straight intervals.
core1a.conditions: One-dimensional conservative potential, positive x to the right, slope defined within each straight segment. 1 J/m=1 N. The force sign does not by itself determine velocity direction.

core1b.title: Your turn: decode a new energy map
core1b.authored_question: An explorer measures the potential energy at four positions on a straight track: (0 m, 2 J), (2 m, 10 J), (4 m, 10 J), and (6 m, 4 J). The graph joins the points with straight lines. What are the conservative force components on the three open sections: 0–2 m, 2–4 m, and 4–6 m?
core1b.change_of_conditions: Unlike the guide's single falling line, the unfamiliar piecewise graph rises, stays flat and falls. The learner has to calculate three slopes, reverse each sign, identify zero-force interval and avoid treating the corners as differentiable.

program.scope_note: Source Q10 remains an unverified scanned theme and is not reproduced. One-dimensional negative gradient relation retained; sharp joins excluded by asking only open intervals.

program.title: Push-apart carts and energy
program.source_gate_note: Initial motion not specified in source
program.learning_goal: Understand signed momentum conservation in a spring-powered push-apart event, and explain that kinetic energy may increase when stored internal energy is released.

core1a.title: A guide: spring-powered toy carts
core1a.authored_question: Two toy carts (1 kg and 3 kg) start at rest together on a smooth track. A compressed spring between them is released. The 1 kg cart rolls right at 3 m/s. Which way does the 3 kg cart move, and how fast?
walkthrough_steps: Set right positive: light cart momentum = 1 × (+3) = +3 kg·m/s.
Conserve total momentum from initial rest: 0 = +3 + 3v, giving v = −1 m/s (heavier cart left).
Check that final momenta +3 and −3 kg·m/s cancel, maintaining the initial total of zero.
Compare total kinetic energy before (0 J) and after (½×1×3² + ½×3×1² = 6 J); stored spring energy supplied the kinetic energy.
core1a.conditions: Initially stationary two-cart system with internal spring release, no significant external horizontal impulse or friction, nonrelativistic motion, right chosen positive.

core1b.title: Your turn: the moving toy cart splits
core1b.authored_question: A 4 kg toy cart is already rolling right at 3 m/s when an internal spring releases and separates it into a 1 kg cart and a 3 kg cart. The 1 kg part rolls right at 6 m/s. The track is smooth and the external horizontal impulse is negligible. What is the 3 kg cart's velocity, and how does the total kinetic energy change?
core1b.change_of_conditions: The guided spring cart pair starts from rest, so total initial momentum is zero; the new independent cart is moving already, with nonzero +12 kg·m/s initial momentum. The learner must conserve nonzero momentum, infer remaining cart speed and independently compare kinetic energy before and after release.
